transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan López (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Nova Head of ML), Daniel Brooks (Nova CTO), Alicia Vega (Nova Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): cost economics; customer budget constraints; technical follow-up to run benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE for your account, and with me is Ethan, our solutions eng. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Rao: Good, thanks. We wanted to dig into the cost side — we're looking at roughly, uh, 1M to 5M tokens a month to start, maybe scale after proof-of-value.
[00:15] Daniel Brooks: Yeah and we have a hard budget for the pilot — roughly $15k / month. Latency needs to be sub-200ms 90th pct on the hot path for our trading signal generation.
[00:25] Ethan López: Cool, thanks Priya. So we'll focus on per-token economics and the knobs — batching, caching, quantization, and whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private makes sense given your latency and data constraints.
[00:35] Alicia Vega: Also want to flag we need VPC connectivity for anything that touches live data. So private/VPC is a requirement for production, but pilot can be hosted if that's cheaper and faster to stand up.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Great. Quick qual — what's your current stack for models? Are you using OpenAI/Anthropic or in-house models?
[00:52] Priya Rao: Mostly Anthropic for generation experiments, some in-house smaller models. We evaluate cost and fidelity right now.
[01:00] Ethan López: Got it. For 1M tokens, the per-token math matters a lot. Redwood hosted has tiered per-token pricing; for example, for a 13B-ish open model equivalent we'd show an illustrative $0.0009 per prompt token and $0.0020 per output token at list for hosted — but your effective unit cost depends on batching and caching.
[01:20] Daniel Brooks: Can you unpack batching and caching? We saw 'batching' in the docs but not sure of real savings.
[01:28] Ethan López: Sure. Batching groups concurrent requests to amortize GPU overhead — so for high QPS workloads batching can bring per-token CPU/GPU time down. For some seq-len distributions we see 20-50% cost reductions. Redwood also does prefix and KV cache: if you have repeated prompts or shared context, KV cache avoids recomputing the earlier tokens so you only pay for new continuation tokens.
[01:50] Priya Rao: Our trading signals share a lot of context — symbol list, last close, some boilerplate. So KV cache sounds promising. But what's the latency hit for cache misses vs hits?
[01:58] Ethan López: Cache hits are basically a read from the KV cache and a much smaller compute path — typically sub-50ms extra. Cache misses go through the full forward pass which is of course longer. We optimize for steady-state by keeping hot prefixes pinned in memory / GPU when in Dedicated.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Important distinction: Hosted versus Dedicated — hosted gives fastest time to market and simple per-token billing, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools which is better for predictable latency and allows pinning hot cache. Private gives full network isolation and KMS integration but has higher onboarding.
[02:33] Daniel Brooks: Economics — at $15k/mo and say 2M tokens, which mode is likely?
[02:40] Ethan López: Rough ballpark: hosted is simple — you pay per-token, no infra commitments. If you hit sustained volume that needs sub-200ms 90th, Dedicated is often cheaper because reserved capacity reduces unit price by, say, 30-60% compared to list hosted per-token in our examples — but you trade off commit and a monthly reserved cost. For 2M tokens, hosted could be within your pilot budget depending on output length, but Dedicated might require a minimum monthly commit (e.g., $10-20k) depending on the GPU profile.
[03:10] Priya Rao: Hmm okay — we don't want a big upfront commit yet. Is there a burst or hybrid option?
[03:15] Maya Chen: Yes — we have burst capacity on Dedicated that lets you handle spikes above commit up to a limit, and we can structure pilot-friendly reserved rates (short-term trial pricing) for first 30-90 days.
[03:27] Alicia Vega: For Private, what's the vendor patch/update cadence? We are enterprise and need a change freeze window.
[03:33] Ethan López: Private deployments can be customer-managed with our control plane; patch cadence is coordinated. Also we support offline/on-prem packages if you need air-gapped.
[03:43] Daniel Brooks: Ok. Can you show a quick per-token example where batching and KV cache change the effective cost?
[03:50] Ethan López: Sure, I'll sketch a simplified example: baseline (no batching/no cache) — assume 100ms per-token-equivalent compute cost; with batching at 20 concurrent request avg we amortize overhead and get down to ~70ms equivalent — that's ~30% compute saving. If 60% of requests hit KV cache then you only compute for 40% of tokens and cache reads are cheap, netting a large reduction. So if your prompts reuse a 150-token prefix a lot, you'll only pay for the continuation tokens.
[04:20] Priya Rao: Makes sense. Any differences in quantization choices? We know quantized models save cost but sometimes hurt latency or quality.
[04:28] Ethan López: Yes — quantization (4-bit/8-bit) reduces memory and can fit larger models on cheaper GPUs. For throughput it often helps cost-per-token significantly but in some workloads there's a small quality delta. For latency-sensitive workloads we balance: lower precision usually reduces compute time slightly but sometimes increases instability for certain models; we recommend an eval/test on your exact prompts.
[04:50] Maya Chen: Also note our Optimize toolkit can recommend quantization profiles based on your evals and expected token distribution.
[04:57] Daniel Brooks: Good. Onboarding — what data residency and logs does Redwood keep for hosted versus private? We have compliance needs.
[05:05] Maya Chen: Hosted will keep logs for the configured retention; data retention, redaction, and customer-controlled KMS for encrypting data-at-rest are available at certain tiers. For strict residency and audit log requirements, Private is preferred — you run in your VPC, keys in your KMS, and we provide audit logs but you control retention. We'll send SOC2/ISO docs after this call.
[05:25] Priya Rao: Can you email an example cost run for 1M/2M/5M tokens with a couple of scenarios: hosted baseline, hosted + batching, dedicated reserved with 6-mo commit, and private overhead?
[05:33] Maya Chen: Absolutely — that's the first action item. We'll include a worked example and assumptions about prompt/response lengths and cache hit rates.
[05:40] Alicia Vega: On the technical bench setup — Ethan, what's the data we need to run the benchmark? We won't share live keys; we'll give sample prompts and a synthetic dataset that mimics distribution.
[05:48] Ethan López: Perfect. For cost benchmark we need a representative set of prompts, expected QPS distribution, and example context reuse patterns. We'll run a 48-hour run and produce per-token cost, latency percentiles, and KV cache hit/miss stats. We'll also show how different batching policies impact latency and cost.
[06:05] Daniel Brooks: Any gotchas — e.g., network egress, storage costs for KV cache?
[06:10] Ethan López: Storage for cache is minimal comparatively; network egress depends on deployment. For Private with VPC peering you'll see standard cloud egress. For Hosted we can minimize by colocating. We'll call out those line items in the pricing sheet.
[06:22] Priya Rao: What's the typical lead time for Private? If we decide to go that route after pilot, what's timeline?
[06:27] Maya Chen: Private deployments typically take 6-8 weeks after procurement for the full on-prem or VPC setup; shorter if we do a hosted pilot and then swap. Dedicated reserved capacity can be provisioned faster, 1-2 weeks in many cases depending on GPU availability.
[06:40] Alicia Vega: Security review — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM?
[06:44] Ethan López: Yes, SAML/SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and audit logs. We'll attach the security whitepaper and our SOC2 link.
[06:55] Priya Rao: Procurement — who on Redwood handles enterprise contracts? We have a standard legal.
[06:59] Maya Chen: Our enterprise sales ops handles contracts; I'll loop in our legal and customer success as we get into committed pricing. For pilot we can do an MSA addendum or a short trial agreement.
[07:08] Daniel Brooks: One more: do you do per-route or per-model throttles to control cost? We need to limit runaway costs in testing.
[07:15] Ethan López: Yes — we expose quotas, per-route rate limits, and per-token ceilings. You can set hard caps and alerts in the console.
[07:23] Priya Rao: Sounds good. If we hit cost issues during pilot, can we switch to a lower-precision model live?
[07:28] Maya Chen: Yes — we support instantaneous fallbacks to model variants or lower precision variants, and routing policies can be automatic based on latency or cost thresholds.
[07:36] Priya Rao: Ok, I think that's the main things. Timeline-wise, procurement wants a pilot starting next week if we can lock pricing quickly.
[07:43] Maya Chen: We'll try to get the pricing deck to you by Friday and Ethan will kick off the benchmark as soon as we have the sample prompts.
[07:50] Daniel Brooks: Great. Thanks.
[07:52] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Quick recap: Maya send pricing + security docs; Ethan run 48-hour benchmark; Alicia share infra constraints; schedule technical deep dive next Thurs.
[08:04] Priya Rao: Yep. Thanks all.

(end of call)
